{{DISPLAYTITLE:Universes and Prop}}
{{Plebeian|Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Why there is no type of all types}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

In Lean every type is itself a term, so every type has a type. The types of types are called
'''universes''' or '''sorts'''. They form a hierarchy: <code>Sort 0</code>,
<code>Sort 1</code>, <code>Sort 2</code> and so on, each a member of the next, with no top.
The bottom level, <code>Sort 0</code>, is <code>Prop</code>, the universe of propositions,
and it obeys different rules from the levels above it. This page sets out the hierarchy, the
rule that assigns a universe to a function type, the operation <math>\mathrm{imax}</math> that
rule needs, universe polymorphism, and the paradox that makes a hierarchy necessary.

== Sorts and their names ==

Each universe has a '''level''', and <code>Sort u</code> is the universe at level
<code>u</code>. Two abbreviations name the cases that matter in practice:
<code>Prop</code> is <code>Sort 0</code>, and <code>Type u</code> is
<code>Sort (u + 1)</code>, with <code>Type</code> alone meaning <code>Type 0</code>, that is,
<code>Sort 1</code>.<ref name="refman-univ">''The Lean Language Reference'', for Lean
4.34.0, lean-lang.org, 2026, section 4.3, "Universes".
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/The-Type-System/Universes/</ref>

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#check Prop
#check Type
#check Type 3
#check Sort 0
example : Sort 0 = Prop := rfl
example : Sort 1 = Type := rfl
example : Sort (3 + 1) = Type 3 := rfl
</pre>

Lean prints <code>Prop : Type</code>, <code>Type : Type 1</code>,
<code>Type 3 : Type 4</code> and <code>Prop : Type</code>, and accepts the three equations
by <code>rfl</code>: the names are notation for the same terms. The typing rule behind the
first four lines is the sort rule of
[[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Terms, types and judgments|Terms, types and judgments]],

:<math>\frac{}{\Gamma \vdash \mathrm{Sort}\,u : \mathrm{Sort}\,(u+1)}</math>

and nothing else gives a universe a type. In particular no universe is a member of itself:

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
example : Type := Type
</pre>

Lean 4.34.1 rejects it:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
Type mismatch
  Type
has type
  Type 1
of sort `Type 2` but is expected to have type
  Type
of sort `Type 1`
</pre>

Lean's universes are also '''not cumulative''': a type in <code>Type 0</code> is not
thereby in <code>Type 1</code>, and each type has exactly one universe.<ref name="refman-univ" />
A type is moved up explicitly, by wrapping it:

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
example : Type 1 := Nat
</pre>

fails with <code>Type mismatch</code>, reporting that <code>Nat</code> has type
<code>Type</code> but is expected to have type <code>Type 1</code>. The standard wrapper is
<code>ULift</code>, a structure with one field, <code>down</code>, whose universe parameter
says how far to lift:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#check (ULift.{1} Nat)
example : Type 1 := ULift.{1} Nat
</pre>

Lean prints <code>ULift Nat : Type 1</code> and accepts the example. Coq, by contrast, has cumulative universes; Carneiro notes that
cumulativity breaks the unique-typing theorem his analysis of Lean relies on.<ref name="carneiro2019">Mario
Carneiro, ''The Type Theory of Lean'', MSc thesis, Carnegie Mellon University, 2019.
https://github.com/digama0/lean-type-theory/releases/tag/v1.0</ref>

== The universe of a function type ==

A dependent function type <code>(x : A) → B</code> is a type, so it lives in some universe.
The formation rule decides which:

:<math>\frac{\Gamma \vdash A : \mathrm{Sort}\,u \qquad \Gamma, x : A \vdash B : \mathrm{Sort}\,v}{\Gamma \vdash (x : A) \to B : \mathrm{Sort}\,(\mathrm{imax}\,u\,v)}</math>

where

:<math>\mathrm{imax}\,u\,v = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } v = 0 \\ \max(u, v) & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}</math>

There are two cases.<ref name="refman-univ" /><ref name="carneiro2019" />

* '''The codomain is data''' (<math>v \geq 1</math>). The function type lives in the larger of the two universes. A type in <code>Type u</code> may only quantify over types in universes no larger than its own; this is '''predicativity'''.
* '''The codomain is a proposition''' (<math>v = 0</math>). The function type is a proposition, whatever the domain. A proposition may quantify over all propositions, or over all types at any level, and still be a proposition; this is '''impredicativity'''.

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#check ∀ (p : Prop), p → p
#check (α : Type) → α → α
#check (α : Type 2) → Prop
#check (n : Nat) → n = n
</pre>

The output is

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
∀ (p : Prop), p → p : Prop
(α : Type) → α → α : Type 1
Type 2 → Prop : Type 3
∀ (n : Nat), n = n : Prop
</pre>

The first statement quantifies over every proposition, including itself, and is a
proposition. The second, the type of the polymorphic identity function on
<code>Type</code>, quantifies over <code>Type</code> and so lands one level up, in
<code>Type 1</code>. The third is a function type into <code>Prop</code>, not a function type
whose values are proofs, so it is data: its codomain <code>Prop</code> lives in
<code>Sort 1</code>, and the result is in <math>\mathrm{Sort}\,(\max(4, 1)) =</math>
<code>Type 3</code>.

== Why imax ==

The two cases could be stated as two rules. A single operation on levels is needed because of
universe polymorphism. A definition may be stated for an arbitrary level variable
<code>v</code>, and the rule must give the function type a universe without knowing whether
<code>v</code> will later be 0. With <math>\max</math> alone that is impossible. The obvious
candidate, <math>\max\,u\,v</math>, goes wrong when <code>v</code> is set to 0: a
proposition that quantifies over a type in <code>Sort u</code> would land in
<math>\mathrm{Sort}\,(\max(u, 0)) = \mathrm{Sort}\,u</math> instead of in
<code>Prop</code>, and <code>Prop</code> would not be impredicative. No other expression
built from <math>\max</math> and successor does better: one that mentions <code>u</code> is
never below <code>u</code>, so it is not 0 when <code>v</code> is 0 and <code>u</code> is
not, and one that does not mention <code>u</code> cannot equal <math>\max(u, v)</math>
for every <code>u</code>. <math>\mathrm{imax}</math> is the level expression that reduces
to the right case once <code>v</code> is known.<ref name="refman-univ" />

Level expressions are built from numerals, variables, successor, <math>\max</math> and
<math>\mathrm{imax}</math>, and two levels are equal when they denote the same number under
every assignment of numbers to their variables.<ref name="carneiro2019" /> Lean will not
treat <math>\mathrm{imax}\,u\,v</math> as <math>\max\,u\,v</math>, because the two differ
when <code>v</code> is 0:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
universe u v

def Fn (α : Sort u) (β : Sort v) : Sort (imax u v) := α → β

#check Fn.{1, 0}
#check Fn.{1, 1}
#check Fn.{0, 2}
</pre>

The three instances print as <code>Fn : Type → Prop → Prop</code>,
<code>Fn : Type → Type → Type</code> and <code>Fn : Prop → Type 1 → Type 1</code>: the
same definition gives a proposition-valued result in the first case and data in the other
two. Stating the result universe as <code>Sort (max u v)</code> instead is rejected:

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
universe u v

def Fn2 (α : Sort u) (β : Sort v) : Sort (max u v) := α → β
</pre>

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
Type mismatch
  α → β
has type
  Sort (imax u v)
of sort `Type (imax u v)` but is expected to have type
  Sort (max u v)
of sort `Type (max u v)`
</pre>

== Universe polymorphism ==

A definition may take '''universe parameters''', written after its name as
<code>.{u, v}</code>. It is then a schema: each use instantiates the parameters with level
expressions, and instantiations at different levels need not be definitionally
equal.<ref name="refman-univ" />

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
set_option pp.universes true in
#check @id
#check @id.{0}
#check List.{0}
</pre>

Lean prints <code>@id.{u_1} : {α : Sort u_1} → α → α</code>, then
<code>@id : ∀ {α : Prop}, α → α</code> for the instance at level 0, where the identity
function on proofs is itself a proof of a proposition, and <code>List : Type → Type</code>.
This is what lets one identity function, one list type and one equality serve at every
level. Without it each would have to be defined once per universe.

== Prop ==

<code>Prop</code> is the universe of propositions. Besides impredicativity, it has
properties that the levels above it lack:<ref name="refman-props">''The Lean Language
Reference'', for Lean 4.34.0, lean-lang.org, 2026, section 4.2, "Propositions".
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/The-Type-System/Propositions/</ref>

* '''Definitional proof irrelevance''': any two proofs of the same proposition are definitionally equal.
* '''Run-time irrelevance''': proofs are erased from compiled code.
* '''Restricted elimination''': except for a class of propositions with at most one proof, a proof cannot be used to produce data, only other proofs.
* '''Extensionality''': logically equivalent propositions are equal, by the axiom <code>propext</code>.

An impredicative universe of propositions is a feature of the Calculus of Constructions of
Coquand and Huet, and the theory implemented by Lean's kernel is a version of that
calculus.<ref name="refman-elab">''The Lean Language Reference'', for Lean 4.34.0,
lean-lang.org, 2026, section 2.3, "The Kernel".
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Elaboration-and-Compilation/</ref><ref name="coc">Thierry Coquand and Gérard Huet, "The calculus of
constructions", ''Information and Computation'' 76(2–3), 1988, pp. 95–120.
https://doi.org/10.1016/0890-5401(88)90005-3</ref><ref name="abelcoquand">Andreas Abel and
Thierry Coquand, "Failure of Normalization in Impredicative Type Theory with Proof-Irrelevant
Propositional Equality", ''Logical Methods in Computer Science'' 16(2), 2020.
https://doi.org/10.23638/LMCS-16(2:14)2020</ref> Its strength is real: Carneiro observes that
impredicativity corresponds, in a set-theoretic model, to having full power sets.<ref name="carneiro2019" />
The restriction on elimination is how the rules ensure that no computation can tell which
proof of a proposition it has received, as proof irrelevance
requires;<ref name="refman-subsing">''The Lean Language Reference'', for Lean 4.34.0,
lean-lang.org, 2026, section 4.4.3.1.1.1, "Subsingleton Elimination".
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/The-Type-System/Inductive-Types/</ref> it is
treated on [[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Proof irrelevance and subsingleton elimination|Proof irrelevance and subsingleton elimination]].

== Why there is a hierarchy ==

The simplest design would be a single universe containing every type, itself included:
<code>Type : Type</code>. That design is inconsistent. In 1972 Girard derived a
contradiction in a type system called System U, by formalising a paradox in the style of
Burali-Forti's paradox of the largest ordinal. The same argument shows that the first version
of Martin-Löf's type theory, which had <code>Type : Type</code>, proves falsity; in type
theory the argument is known as '''Girard's paradox'''.<ref name="nlab">nLab, "Burali-Forti's paradox", section "In type theory: Girard's
paradox", revision of 24 November 2023. https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Girard%27s+paradox</ref><ref name="hurkens">Antonius
J. C. Hurkens, "A simplification of Girard's paradox", in ''Typed Lambda Calculi and
Applications'' (TLCA 1995), Lecture Notes in Computer Science 902, Springer, 1995,
pp. 266–278. https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0014058</ref> The ''Homotopy Type Theory'' book makes
the same point for a universe that contains itself: every type, including the empty one,
becomes inhabited.<ref name="hott">The Univalent Foundations Program, ''Homotopy Type
Theory: Univalent Foundations of Mathematics'', Institute for Advanced Study, 2013,
section 1.3, "Universes and families". https://homotopytypetheory.org/book/</ref>

Hurkens's paper locates the problem precisely. Higher-order logic, in which propositions may
quantify over all propositions, is consistent. Adding a single rule, which lets a type be
formed by quantifying over the sort of all types, gives the system called
<math>\lambda U^-</math>, which Coquand had already shown inconsistent; Hurkens gives a short
term in it whose type is falsity.<ref name="hurkens" /> Impredicativity for propositions
alone is therefore consistent, and adding it for types as well is not. Lean's design
follows the line exactly: <code>Prop</code> is impredicative, and every universe above it is
predicative and contained in the next. The plain-language account is
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Why there is no type of all types|Why there is no type of all types]].

How strong the resulting hierarchy is, measured against set theory, is the subject of
[[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Consistency and the metatheory|Consistency and the metatheory]].
